newsitem.title: USA: U.S. space shuttle Atlantis leaves Russia's Mir.
newsitem.headline: U.S. space shuttle Atlantis leaves Russia's Mir.

text.p: The space shuttle Atlantis uncoupled from Russia's Mir space station on Wednesday after swapping NASA crewmen and replenishing supplies.
Atlantis slipped the metallic grip of Mir's docking port at 9:04 p.m. EDT (0104 GMT) as the two craft soared into the sunrise 245 miles (395 km) above western Russia.
"Houston, we have separation," shuttle skipper Charles Precourt told mission control as four springs gently nudged Atlantis away from Mir.

Pilot Eileen Collins, who became NASA's first female shuttle pilot in 1995, then fired thrusters to separate the two craft. The two crews sung a traditional Russian cosmonaut song as Atlantis departed.
"We apologize if we were a little out of tune," Precourt said. "Probably means we ought to keep our day jobs."

The shuttle left behind British-born astronaut Michael Foale for a four-month tour of duty aboard the Russian orbital outpost. Foale replaces NASA's Jerry Linenger, who has lived and worked aboard the station since January.
Atlantis also delivered a record 4,000 lbs (1,814 kg) of supplies and equipment, including a new device for generating breathing oxygen and repair gear to plug leaks in the station's cooling systems.
The shuttle was hauling away 2,630 lbs (1,193 kg) of scientific results, broken equipment and trash. Linenger and six crewmates were scheduled to return to Earth aboard Atlantis on Saturday.
Earlier on Wednesday, the shuttle crew had said farewell to Foale and his Russian crewmates, Vasily Tsibliev and Alexander Lazutkin, and one by one floated back aboard Atlantis.
"We'll see you," Precourt told the waving Mir crew before the tunnel linking the two craft was swung shut.
"We've wished them well," he radioed mission control. "Just kind of sorry to see them close the hatch."
Before the hatches closed, Linenger gave mission control a televised tour of Mir, his home for 122 days, and recalled the events of Feb. 23 when a serious fire broke out.
Fighting the fire was difficult because of the station's cramped conditions and visibility was near zero, he explained.
"You could sort of see your fingers if you looked hard," he said. "It was very, very dense smoke. An interesting experience, something you don't want to repeat, of course."
The blaze also blocked the route to one of the Soyuz spacecraft that would have been needed to evacuate the station.
"It would have been very difficult to get through the flame itself to get to one of the rescue vehicles," he said. At the time of the fire there were six crew members aboard the station.
During the tour, Linenger pointed out the space station's emergency breathing masks. They "saved our lives" he said.
The fire was the first in a string of mechanical breakdowns that marred Linenger's stay aboard Mir. Problems with the life support systems and leaks in the cooling systems followed.
NASA approved Foale's stay on Mir after most of the malfunctions were corrected. The 40-year-old astrophysicist said he had no qualms about living aboard the rickety, 11-year-old space station.

"As far as my worries, I don't really have any right now," Foale told a news conference on Wednesday. "As long as we keep working hard with the ground and keep the supplies coming, we can maintain these things."
As for Linenger, he had one concrete plan after returning to Earth: "I'm going fishing," he said.
